newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil's Cardoso will need new-found muscle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil's Cardoso will need new-found muscle.

text.p: Brazil's government proved its muscle by winning three key victories in a month-long special session of Congress due to end on Friday. But political analysts saw pitfalls ahead for its centerpiece reform program.
"Nothing can be taken for granted in Brazil," said Murillo Aragao of consultants Arko Advice, warning of possible rebellions by disgruntled members of government-allied parties.
"The government is going to have to do a lot of peacemaking and appear magnanimous to the losers," he said.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso won his third of three key tests in Congress on Wednesday when the Chamber of Deputies chose reform-minded deputy Michel Temer as its new president.

A day earlier, the Senate elected as president Sen. Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, another Cardoso ally. And last week, a bill allowing the president to run for a second term in 1998 was approved in a first of two votes in the Chamber of Deputies.

A cartoon in financial daily Gazeta Mercantil showed Cardoso as a colossus towering over a miniscule Congress. But observers said the president would have to be quick if he was to take full political advantage of his victories and press on with reforms.
"There are black clouds on the distant horizon in the form of the 1998 elections," said a government deputy.

If re-election was fully approved by Congress, as expected, Cardoso would cruise to a win. But the race for state governorships will turn Cardoso's allies against one another 12 months before the elections, he added.

Seeking to seize the initiative, the government hopes to hold a second and final vote on re-election in the lower house after next week's Carnival holiday, followed by a first vote on its civil service reform bill in the first half of March.
And last week, Sen. Benavides Veras was appointed to oversee a pension reform bill, currently awaiting a rewrite in the Senate after being watered down in voting by deputies last July.
But Congress-watchers said they sensed more than a whiff of rebellion in the lower house in Temer's election victory.
He won 257 of a total 504 votes cast, less than triumphant predictions of 300 and only four more than the minimum needed to win the election in a first round.
"The government's feathers were ruffled," columnist Tereza Cruvinel wrote in newspaper O Globo. "(Temer's victory) was a goal, but the ball hit the crossbar before entering the net."
Government sources said they expected Temer to take a more conciliatory approach than his predecessor, Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes, renowned for his steamroller approach to politics.
"Temer's more inclined to look for the consensus and does not share Luiz Eduardo's free-market convictions...But he's got it easier because heads are more mature these days," Brandt said.

He recalled how even the president's Brazilian Social Democratic Party and its staunchest ally, the Liberal Front Party, clashed regularly when Magalhaes assumed the lower house presidency in 1995 at the start of Cardoso's term.

Congress-watchers said they also expected a change of style in the way the Senate is run, after the election of Luiz Eduardo's powerful father as its new president, taking over from former president Jose Sarney, a stickler for the rules.
"(Antonio Carlos Magalhaes) could turn out to be our best friend or a heck of a problem," said a government source.
Magalhaes senior emerged as a political force in the 1964-85 dictatorship and backed every civilian government since then.

But his first loyalty remains to his own power base in impoverished Bahia state. In 1995, he held up a $1.2 billion air surveillance system for the Amazon until the government bailed out failed bank Banco Economico, which is based in Bahia.
Shortly after his victory on Tuesday, Magalhaes hinted he wanted to restrict Cardoso's ability to put laws into immediate effect via decrees, sidestepping long-winded debate in Congress.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 5561 2230358))
